form.2. SHORT COURSE DESCRIPTION: A second programming course that moves students from writing small single-file programs to building larger applications made of several components with clear interfaces. Students learn object-oriented design, how to write code that others can reuse and test, how to structure programs around established design patterns, and how to handle errors, input/output and concurrency. By the end, students working in pairs can take a reasonably well-specified application design and deliver a working, tested, multi-component program. Java is the vehicle, but the course is about program design, not the Java language.
form.3. TOPICS / CONTENT AREAS:
Treatment of this list: starting hypotheses — may add/drop/reorder with justification.
A. Object-oriented foundations: classes and objects, encapsulation, modularity, object relationships (association, composition), interfaces
B. Inheritance and polymorphism: inheritance hierarchies, abstract classes, polymorphism via interfaces and inheritance, method resolution, immutability
C. Generic and reusable code: generics, comparing and cloning objects, the collections framework
D. Robust programs: exception handling, assertions, defensive and secure programming, I/O streams and serialization
E. Testing and tooling: unit testing, debugging, version control as part of everyday development
F. Designing before coding: use cases, UML class/sequence/use-case diagrams, object-oriented design of a problem
G. Event-driven programming and GUIs
H. Concurrency: threads, thread pools, mutual exclusion, race conditions and deadlocks, producer-consumer, speedup
I. Design patterns: common creational, structural and behavioural patterns applied to real problems
form.4. COURSE INTENT:
Central question the course answers: How do you design, build and test a multi-component program so that its parts can be developed independently and reused?
Pedagogical emphasis: design thinking before coding; writing code others can read, reuse and test; learning by building a substantial team project.
This course should NOT become:
- a Java language features course
- a data-structures course (that is covered by the prerequisite)
- a lecture-only course without regular hands-on practice
form.5. TARGET STUDENTS:
Programmes: B.Tech. CSE (core course); also taken by other B.Tech. programmes
Year: 2nd year (3rd semester)
Assumed background: CSE101 Introduction to Programming and CSE102 Data Structures and Algorithms — comfortable with procedural programming, functions, arrays, lists, recursion and basic data structures
form.6. EXPECTED LEVEL / COURSE CODE: 2xx level (second-year core); code to be assigned
form.8. L-T-P / CONTACT HOURS: 3-1-0 (three lecture hours and one tutorial hour per week)

form.11. LAB / PRACTICAL COMPONENT:
Lab required: no separate lab slot; hands-on practice happens in tutorials and take-home work
Available infrastructure: students' own laptops; Java JDK, an IDE (Eclipse/IntelliJ), JUnit, Git/GitHub; TAs for tutorials
form.12. ASSESSMENT PREFERENCES:
Preferred components: short take-home programming assignments, a pair-programming course project with milestones, quizzes, mid-sem and end-sem exams
Components to avoid: none
Rationale: the course is about building software, so a substantial share of the grade should come from programming work, while exams check individual understanding
